steps.explanationAfterStep: Homolytic cleavage: each fish-hook moves one electron.
The Br• formed here carries the chain on.

title: Radical bromination — propagation
subtitle: Br• abstracts a hydrogen from methane; the methyl radical takes Br from Br₂
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press)

reactants.caption: bromine radical + methane + Br₂
hintTiers: Radical steps move single electrons. Which bond does Br• attack?
Br• forms a bond to H while the C–H bond breaks evenly: one electron to each partner. Count the electrons: three fish-hooks.
Br• electron → Br–H; one C–H electron → Br–H; the other C–H electron → C.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Use fish-hook arrows: each moves one electron.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Bonding Br to carbon would need a fifth bond on C. Br• abstracts a hydrogen, which can have only one bond.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One fish-hook per electron: the new H–Br bond needs two electrons, one from Br• and one from the C–H bond.

methyl-radical.caption: HBr + methyl radical + Br₂
hintTiers: The methyl radical needs an electron partner. Which weak bond is nearby?
CH₃• forms a C–Br bond while the Br–Br bond breaks evenly. Three fish-hooks.
C• electron → C–Br; one Br–Br electron → C–Br; the other → Br.
methyl-radical.learnerPrompt: The methyl radical reacts with Br₂.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That reverses the previous step. Br₂ has a much weaker bond than H–Br, so the chain continues with Br₂.

mechanismSummary: Two propagation steps. Each consumes one radical and makes another, so a single initiation event brominates many molecules.
